content: The applicability of the recommendations should be carefully evaluated in relation to local health workers, the available service delivery models, and the regulatory frameworks in place. Adaptation of these recommendations must involve consultation with a diverse range of stakeholders, including policymakers, local health workers, professional societies, civil society organizations, and individuals with chronic primary low back pain (CPLBP) and their families. Implementing these considerations will require active commitments and actions from governments and relevant stakeholders. Monitoring the implementation of these initiatives and sharing experiences and resources both within and across countries can support national and global efforts to implement these recommendations effectively. For interventions where a conditional recommendation against routine delivery has been made, discontinuation of such practices is advised in most contexts. Conversely, for interventions with a conditional recommendation in favor, health workers are encouraged to select and sequence interventions based on the individual needs and preferences of the person with CPLBP, guided by a biopsychosocial assessment. Given the multifactorial and complex etiology of CPLBP, a single intervention in isolation may not be sufficient to provide benefit. This underscores the need for countries to offer a comprehensive suite of effective intervention options. Health workers should be able to select, tailor, and sequence these interventions according to the unique needs and circumstances of individuals, informed by a biopsychosocial perspective, shared decision-making, and contextual considerations related to the local health system. Universal health coverage (UHC) aims to ensure that all individuals and communities receive the full spectrum of essential, quality health services they need throughout their lives without financial hardship. Strengthening and reorienting health systems toward primary health care (PHC) is critical for achieving UHC. PHC is the most inclusive, equitable, cost-effective, and efficient approach to improving physical and mental health, as well as social well-being. CPLBP is a common reason for seeking care in primary health care settings. Non-surgical interventions for adults with CPLBP can feasibly be delivered in these settings, supported by appropriate referral and care pathways. However, in many national health systems, musculoskeletal health, including low back pain, is not identified as a public health priority or a priority condition at the population level or in specific groups, such as younger and older people. This lack of prioritization may limit opportunities for governments to optimize the management of CPLBP and its integration within UHC. Governments and relevant stakeholders must commit to elevating the priority level of musculoskeletal health within health systems and take action on CPLBP to facilitate the implementation of these guidelines into practice. This should be coupled with a policy response that includes broad dissemination of the guidelines, targeted public health messaging, and leveraging cross-sectoral partnerships to increase awareness about recommended care for people with CPLBP, as well as care that is not recommended. Health workers delivering care for adults, including older individuals, with CPLBP require skills and knowledge in assessment, diagnosis, and clinical management, particularly in relation to person-centered chronic pain care from a biopsychosocial perspective and behavior change methods. Building workforce capacity within primary and community care settings will be necessary to deliver recommended interventions and discontinue care that is not recommended, such as traction, therapeutic ultrasound, TENS, lumbar braces, belts, and certain medications like opioid analgesics, antidepressants, and anticonvulsants. Support for assessing current workforce capacities and opportunities for expanding cadres will be essential. Emphasis should be placed on encouraging evidence-based chronic pain care and providing technical guidance in assessment, diagnosis, and care pathways, including validated and locally available tools to inform assessment and care planning from a biopsychosocial perspective. Health workers from various disciplines may be involved in the care of people with CPLBP. Establishing care standards and competencies that are transdisciplinary and informed by the guidelines can reduce unwarranted care variation and the delivery of ineffective care. Health systems must support the delivery of multidisciplinary care to develop and monitor high-quality, person-centered care. Long-term planning is needed for resource generation and budget allocation to support healthy aging, rehabilitation, physical activity, and the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases. Governments may need to assess systemand service-level readiness and capacity to act on CPLBP and integrate evidence-based interventions into local service delivery. Recommended interventions may not be available in all settings due to regulatory frameworks, workforce capacity, or financial constraints. Countries must strengthen system and service delivery capabilities to ensure the availability, accessibility, and affordability of recommended interventions, such as multicomponent biopsychosocial care, psychological interventions, certain medicines, and other non-pharmacological interventions. Additionally, efforts should support the scaling down of interventions that are conditionally not recommended. Processes and outcomes of implementation activities should be monitored and documented, including coverage, service use, and health outcomes. Developing or revising national guidelines and care standards for CPLBP to guide local service delivery models may be required. In many countries, service models and referral pathways for CPLBP may not be well-established or developed. Co-creation of service models, including appropriate referral pathways, that are locally acceptable, feasible, and explicitly address equity in access to care will be necessary to operationalize recommendations at the service and clinical levels. Co-creation should involve individuals with CPLBP, health workers, civil society, and other groups, following practices recommended by WHO for integrated people-centered health services and frameworks for meaningful engagement of people living with non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions. Similarly, co-creation of accurate public health messaging about care for CPLBP will be important. Addressing the shortage of health workers to strengthen and sustain high-quality services for CPLBP management will require collaboration with education and training institutions. This will ensure that the guiding principles and recommendations, as well as any future updates, are reflected in clinical training for preand post-licensure health practitioner education. Curricula must align with evolving standards for person-centered chronic pain care. Research efforts must address substantial limitations in the certainty of available evidence across interventions, largely due to a lack of high-quality trials. Future research should prioritize high-quality trials in areas where evidence gaps exist, focusing on interventions for CPLBP care. Trials should include diverse population groups, such as older individuals, and measure outcomes meaningful to people with CPLBP and their care providers. Observational research from population-level health registries in countries at all levels of economic development is needed, particularly to monitor harms associated with interventions. Implementation research evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of interventions across settings will be important for informing future global guidance in CPLBP care. High-quality primary qualitative studies from lower-income countries are particularly needed to inform global guidelines. Knowledge gaps exist for specific population groups, including older individuals and marginalized or vulnerable groups. Trials often exclude older individuals with comorbidities or those in long-term care facilities, creating a knowledge gap regarding the care of more vulnerable older people. Research should ensure that cohorts are representative of real-world contexts to enhance clinical relevance and transferability of findings.
